name: Hair clippers

lead: Hair clippers are motorised devices with a moving blade that cuts hair to a chosen length. Barbers and home users use them for buzz cuts, short back and sides, tapers and fades.

For looks, a cleanly clipped cut with even length and tidy edges can make hair look deliberate and groomed, and a close or faded cut can frame the face and skull shape. Guards and blade sizes set the length.

paras: Users choose a guard or blade size for the desired length, work in sections and blend lengths for tapers or fades. Clippers are oiled or sprayed to keep blades running smoothly. Many men use them at home on a regular schedule between barber visits.
Risks are minor: nicks and irritation from very close cutting, and shared or unclean blades can spread skin infections. Manufacturers advise cleaning and lubricating blades.

angle.text: Clippers give a precise, repeatable length and blend, which defines the outline of a short haircut.

lead: Hair clippers are electric or manual cutting tools in which one comb-like blade slides against another to cut hair to a set length. They are the main tool behind buzz cuts, short back and sides, tapers and fades, where length is set by a guard or blade size and blended from longer hair on top to very short hair near the ears and neck [1][2].

For appearance, clippers give an even, repeatable length and clean edges, which is what makes a short cut look deliberate. A close or tapered cut can make the face look more defined and is also described as suiting people with thinning or receding hairlines [3]. Many people use clippers at home on a regular schedule between barber visits, and barbers use them for edging, siding and fades [2].

Manual clippers date from around 1855 and are credited to the Serbian barber Nikola Bizumić; the first electric clipper was patented by Leo J. Wahl by 1921, with Andis entering the market in 1921 and Oster in 1928 [1].
infobox: About 0.1 mm to 19 mm (Oster blade sizes) [1]
Oil or clipper spray; some stainless blades need no oil [1]

paras: A clipper has a pair of sharpened, comb-like blades held in close contact; one slides sideways against the other to cut the hair between the teeth, and low friction through material, finish and lubrication is important to how well it works [1]. Electric clippers use one of three motor types. Magnetic and pivot designs use electromagnetic force from copper windings around steel with a spring returning the blade, and rotary motors can run on direct or alternating current [1]. Most consumer magnetic clippers use a vibrating motor tuned to a resonant frequency, and a side screw retunes it if it becomes loud [1].
Blades are usually rust-resistant stainless steel. Ceramic blades do not corrode and stay sharp longer, but are brittle and more expensive to replace [1].

Oster blade sizes run from very fine zero blades (from about 0.1 mm) through medium and full coarse blades to long blades of 5/8 and 3/4 inch (about 19 mm). Regrowth estimates in the reference range from about five hours for the finest blades to roughly five to six weeks for the longest [1]. Guard numbers work on a similar logic: hair grows about one-eighth inch per week, so a number 1 guard leaves roughly a week's growth, a number 2 two weeks', and so on [2].
Zero-range blades, from #000000 to #0A, leave hair from about 1/250 to 3/64 inch and are used for fine tapers and edges [2].

A buzz cut, also called a wiffle cut, is a very short style with roughly equal length across the head; related styles include the brush cut, crew cut and flat top [3]. Wikipedia describes the rise of the style as linked to manual clippers, which let barbers cut quickly and close [3]. Recruits in the armed forces of several countries, including Australia, China, Russia, the United Kingdom and the United States, receive buzz cuts at the start of training, a practice that originally aimed to prevent head lice and is now described as being for easy maintenance, cooling and uniformity [3]. It has also been worn by public figures including Sinead O'Connor and Natalie Portman, and has been described as a protest against standards of feminine beauty [3].

A short taper, also called a fade, uses a coarse clipper on the sides and back up to nearly the crown, arced at the hat band, with finer clipper work blended out toward the edges [2]. Taper lengths range from short through semi-short (half crown), medium, long and extra long, defined by where the sideburns end and how far up the sides are shortened [2]. Barbering texts divide a cut into edging (the lower hairline around the sideburns, ears and nape), siding and topping, with edging done first; edging is usually done with clippers, siding with shears over comb, and topping with shears over fingers [2]. The nape can be tapered to the skin or squared in a block [2].

Manual clippers, operated by squeezing paired handles, were invented around 1855 by Bizumić and made short cuts fast; they became associated with schoolboys, soldiers and prisoners, and are still used by some barbers, including extensively in India for short back and sides [1]. In Greece male students had their heads shaved with manual clippers from the early twentieth century until the practice ended in 1982 [1].

Leo J. Wahl began by designing a handheld massager for his uncle's company in Sterling, Illinois, then saw an opening to improve barbers' tools and patented an electric clipper by 1921, the year the firm became Wahl Clipper Corporation; he died in 1957 with more than 100 patent applications [1]. Mathew Andis Sr. entered the electric clipper market by 1921, selling door to door, then co-founded Andis O M Manufacturing with John Oster and Henry Meltzer before founding the Andis Clipper Company [1]. John Oster Manufacturing entered in 1928 and was acquired by Sunbeam in 1960 [1]. Wahl, Andis and Oster are still the main names [1]. The short back and sides style that clippers make easy has older roots in Roman legionary hair regulation and in the businessman cut of the twentieth century [2].

Metal blades are usually oiled often, and manufacturers sell their own oils; Wahl's is described as essentially mineral oil [1]. Aerosol clipper sprays can cool, disinfect, lubricate and clean, and some clippers have hard stainless blades that need no oiling [1].

Wikipedia notes that Orthodox Jews tend to avoid clipping the sides of the head and that some Muslim men consider cutting more than a fistful of beard forbidden, which bears on how clippers are used by some groups [1].

Outside styling, clippers are used in hospitals to remove hair before surgery. A 1983 randomised trial of 1,013 patients undergoing elective operations compared shaving with clipping the night before or the morning of surgery and reported significantly fewer wound infections with morning-of clipping [4]. A randomised comparison of clippers and razors has also been published for pre-operative hair removal on the male genitalia [5].

No studies found on clippers as a grooming aid. In surgical settings, a 1983 randomised trial of 1,013 patients reported fewer wound infections with morning-of clipping than with shaving [4], and a randomised trial compared clippers with razors for pre-operative hair removal on the male genitalia [5].

timeline.event: Manual clippers invented by Serbian barber Nikola Bizumić [1].
Leo Wahl takes over his uncle's Sterling, Illinois business while his uncle serves in the Spanish-American War [1].
Wahl's electric clipper design patented and the Wahl Clipper Corporation named; Andis enters the market [1].
John Oster Manufacturing enters the clipper market [1].
Greece ends the practice of shaving male students' heads with manual clippers [1].
